question: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are water-, fat- and heat-resistant chemicals and are found in many everyday products. They do not break down easily and therefore accumulate over time in soil, water, plants, animals and ultimately in humans. These ‘forever chemicals’ are highly toxic to humans and the environment. Among other things, they have an effect on hormones, damage the immune system, impair fertility and can cause cancer. Wind farms continually contaminate their surroundings with PFAS. These are found, inter alia, in the coatings of the blades, which are exposed to abrasion, as well as in transmissions, storage systems, lubricants, hydraulic fluids and cable insulation. As a result, more than 200 chemicals, including PFAS, are released from wind turbines into the air, soil, gardens, surface water and groundwater. Denmark and Sweden have recognised the risk and introduced significantly stricter limits than the European Union for certain PFAS – these limits being 25 and 50 times lower, respectively. 1.
What does the Commission intend to do to finally ban PFAS?
What does the Commission intend to do to stop the ongoing contamination of humans, animals and the environment by PFAS from wind turbines?
What is the Commission’s position regarding the numerous statements by environmental experts and doctors that the current EU limits for PFAS are far too high?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.9.2026) A restriction proposal covering all per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) was submitted by five national authorities1 under the Regulation concerning the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH)2 in 2023. This proposal, universal in its scope (i.e. covering all PFAS), is currently being assessed by the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA). Wind turbines are one of the sub-uses under the energy sector assessed in detail during this process in terms of risk, availability of alternatives and socioeconomic impacts3. However, the risk assessment is carried out per (sub)use and not necessarily per individual technology. Once finalised, ECHA’s Committees’ final opinions will be the basis for the Commission to prepare a restriction proposal for the placing on the market and use of PFAS, taking into account all relevant information. While waiting for ECHA’s final scientific assessment, the Commission cannot anticipate how the use of PFAS in wind turbines will be addressed. Nonetheless, as announced in the Chemicals Industry Action Plan4, the Commission is fully committed to minimising PFAS emissions and addressing the pollution caused by PFAS to protect the health of EU citizens and the environment. Where adequate alternatives in terms of performance and safety are not available, the continued use of PFAS in industrial applications may be allowed for critical applications, under specific conditions until acceptable substitutes are found. Possible derogations for uses of PFAS will need to be accompanied by requirements to reduce emissions at all lifecycle stages to limit the release of pollutants into the environment and by clear incentives to innovate towards finding alternatives.
